accuracy.evidence: Rock facts checked against the British Geological Survey 'How rocks form' pages and the Geological Society rock cycle resources: igneous rock forms from cooled magma (intrusive, e.g. granite with large crystals from slow cooling) or lava (extrusive, e.g. basalt with small crystals, pumice with vesicles from gas); sedimentary rock forms by deposition, compaction and cementation of sediment (sandstone, mudstone, limestone, chalk from coccolith remains) and younger layers lie above older ones (superposition); metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change rock in the solid state (mudstone or shale to slate, limestone to marble, sandstone to quartzite). The lab's 'melts' zone sends the rock to magma, matching the rule that melting leads to igneous rock. Parameterised answers a, 2*a and 1 are whole numbers at every corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets slips documented for KS2 rocks (Ofsted and ASE primary science notes, BGS teacher guidance): metamorphic rock is melted rock (the heat bar's Melts zone with 'melted rock cools into igneous rock', predict 3, robot saying 4, m5, challenge 'melt'), fossils are in any rock (predict 2, p4, challenge 'fossil'), the top layer is oldest (predict 1, the oldest-layer tap with 'that layer settled last, so it is the youngest', robot saying 3, p1, m1, challenge 'old'), and rocks are all the same or sorted by colour (the sorting cards give how each formed).

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab models the three ways rocks form: drop sand, mud and shells into a sea tank and drag a weight down to press them (shells become fossils), choose surface or deep underground for granite, basalt and pumice from their crystal clues, drag a heat marker across warm, hot and melts zones to turn limestone, mudstone and sandstone into marble, slate and quartzite, then sort textured rock cards. flagrock (932, ages 5-7) only digs to bedrock and sorts rock versus not rock; the fossil labs (543, 893) cover fossilisation, not rock types. The lab_distinct gate keeps flag_rocktype.js under 30% similar to every lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child makes each rock type and sees the cause: layers they chose stack in order, so when asked for the oldest layer they can see it is the first one they dropped; pushing the heat marker into Melts turns the rock to magma with the reason, so the 'not melted' rule is felt, not told; picking surface for granite gets 'big crystals need a long, slow cool'. Each sort card gives a clue about formation, and a wrong bin gets that type's formation rule.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option: 'Which layer is the oldest?' (top layer) before the child builds and presses layers, 'Could you find a fossil in rock made from lava?' (yes, often) before the igneous scene, and 'To make metamorphic rock, do you melt the rock?' (yes) before the heat bar, where melting is refused. The step completion message reveals the child's own prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions, each with two tagged wrong answers. why() has six distinct messages: fossil (living things buried in mud or sand make sedimentary rock), ign (cooled magma or lava is igneous), old (new layers settle on top), melt (heated and squeezed but not melted), met (marble is changed limestone) and sed (grains or shells pressed in layers). Each names the slip and gives the fix.

readability.evidence: Kid text keeps to short sentences and explains each term as it appears (magma, lava, crystals, layers) and passes the family kid FK limit; the adult text uses igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic, compaction terms and passes the adult limit. Canvas signs shrink to fit at 360 px and rock names sit in white pills over the textures.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one thing: the three types are named by how they form, igneous with the granite and basalt crystal contrast, sedimentary with layers, oldest at the bottom and fossils, and metamorphic as changed rock with two examples. The adult text gives the Year 3 requirement and key words, the formation science with examples, three named mistakes with what to ask, and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler and under 12% overlap with every other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots in dark theme at rest and part-way through each Show me: the sea tank takes 60% of the width with three large sediment buckets beside it, the weight sits on the layers once dragged, the pressed layers and the oldest-layer highlight are clear, the two cooling places are half-width cards with words above their pictures, the heat bar spans the canvas with a 22 px strip and a big marker, and the three sort bins share one row. Every canvas action has a button twin.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button: Drop sand, mud or shells, Press the weight down, each layer named by its position and sediment, On the surface or Deep underground, Cooler, Hotter and Heat and squeeze, the three rock-type bins named with the rock, and Right or Slip. Every result and the heat level are spoken through c.say and the canvas aria-label; challenge feedback is a polite live region. Rock types are named in words, never by colour alone. The walk gate's axe run is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
